item.title: Going cashless demands more digital security. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The near-doubling of payment cards across Bangladesh over the past five years -- surging to nearly 53 million cards alongside an even bigger leap in total transaction values -- signals a profound shift toward a more cashless, digitized economy. This is a positive, especially for a nation that has long aspired to more effective digitization.
According to recent Bangladesh Bank data, debit, credit, and prepaid instruments have all become deeply embedded in urban and retail consumer behaviour. Yet, we cannot ignore the fact that this rapid financial modernization brings with it urgent structural challenges.
While the proliferation of cashless options broadens financial access, it also exposes systemic vulnerabilities within our digital financial ecosystem. Consumer cybersecurity education, fraud protection mechanisms, and robust merchant infrastructure have not kept pace with this rapid adoption, and as more citizens transition to electronic payments, cybersecurity threats have the potential to undermine public trust in the digital banking architecture.
Furthermore, the widening gap in cross-border card usage -- where outward spending by Bangladeshis abroad drastically outstrips foreign card spending within the country -- highlights ongoing pressures on foreign exchange reserves and capital flight concerns, and cannot be entirely dismissed.
As such, the central bank, and our financial sector at large, must move beyond celebrating raw adoption metrics. True digital financial inclusion requires unyielding regulatory oversight and a cybersecurity apparatus that protects people from threats.
A modernized payment system is only as strong as its weakest security link. As such, it is imperative that we do not fail to guarantee absolute protection for digital transactions. The promise of a cashless economy only exists when those who are to benefit from it are protected.

item.title: We need good teachers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We are troubled by a recent report in this newspaper revealing a deep-seated crisis in our government schools, where severe staffing shortages, acute leadership deficits, and an absence of subject-specialist educators are all but crippling classroom learning.
When over 27,000 of the roughly 65,000 primary headteacher posts sit vacant nationwide, and even more assistant teacher slots in secondary schools remain unfilled, the commitment to building a competitive, modern workforce rings entirely hollow.
When a handful of teachers are responsible for the education of hundreds of students, it is no wonder then that the standards fall. We cannot be blaming educators when they are forced to manage classes of such numbers while simultaneously burdened with tedious daily administrative paperwork
Compounding this structural vacuum, official recently published data from the Bangladesh Bureau of Educational Information and Statistics (BANBEIS) shows that over 52% of government secondary school teachers lack basic professional pedagogical training.
To that end, expecting understaffed, untrained, and administratively overwhelmed teachers to deliver high-quality instruction is an absurd strategy destined for failure.
This paralysis stems directly from bureaucratic inertia, prolonged recruitment delays, and an utter lack of strategic planning. While state officials frequently boast about digital initiatives and infrastructure expansions, they consistently ignore the fundamental pillar of learning: Qualified, well-supported teachers. Brick-and-mortar classrooms mean nothing without competent educators to guide the students inside them.
This crisis must be confronted with unyielding urgency. Stopgap measures and delayed hiring drives will no longer suffice. It is time to eliminate administrative bottlenecks and aggressively fill all vacant teaching and administrative positions.
Crucially, we also need rigorous, mandatory pre-service training and competitive incentives to attract better talent into the teaching profession, along with eliminating offering jobs to those who are unqualified.
Education will only be the backbone of our economy if we do not sacrifice the future of our youth to bureaucratic complacency regarding teachers.

item.title: Living with the deluge. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As the monsoon winds down each year, the conversation around urban waterlogging in Bangladesh begins to fade. The rains eventually ease, the streets become dry, and the images of submerged roads and stranded commuters gradually disappear from our screens. Until the next heavy downpour brings them all back.
That is perhaps the most predictable part of Bangladesh's urban waterlogging crisis. Every monsoon, we go through the same cycle: Heavy rain, flooded streets, public frustration, a flurry of criticism and promises, followed by a return to business as usual once the water recedes.
What is missing is a sustained effort to understand why our cities remain so vulnerable and, more importantly, what can be done differently.
For a glimpse of what this cycle means on the ground, consider a familiar scene in Dhaka's Shantinagar neighbourhood.
For local shopkeepers, the heavy monsoon rain offers little relief from the heat. Instead, it signals a familiar scramble to protect their goods. Sacks of wholesale rice are quickly pulled onto higher wooden pallets, expensive electronics are moved onto top shelves, and makeshift sandbags are dragged to storefronts.
Within 45 minutes, the asphalt street became a stagnant urban river. Rickshaws pushed through waist-deep water as passengers lifted their belongings above it. This was a routine afternoon in July, not the aftermath of a super-cyclone.
Yet we have normalized this seasonal flooding as the inevitable price of living in a rapidly expanding metropolis. The problem is not simply the rain, but how poorly we manage it.
In recent years, the discourse in our cities has at least begun to shift. People are slowly moving away from blaming the clouds with a growing recognition of realities on the ground, that the aging drains and sinking ground are as much to blame as the sky. Naming the problem is merely step one; solving it is the real challenge.
The global North has embraced the “sponge city” model, using permeable surfaces, continuous mechanical sweeping, and underground systems to absorb and store rainwater. But importing this model into cities burdened by silt, dust, waste, and weak maintenance systems would be a recipe for quick failure.
If our concrete drains already struggle with solid waste, we need an approach suited to our own reality. That means moving from trying to keep water out, to a cooperative approach of giving it safe spaces to go.
Singapore turned this idea into reality at Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park. It replaced a 2.7 km concrete canal, once known as “ the long drain ,” with a winding, planted river through a public park. Its banks use roots and rock instead of concrete, allowing the river to spread across the park during heavy rain, slow down and drain without flooding nearby neighborhoods. In dry weather, the same space becomes a lawn for families and children.
What is striking is the cost. The greener river was about 15% cheaper than rebuilding the concrete, while carrying more water and the wildlife rose by roughly a third . Working with the water was the cheaper option whereas fighting it was the more expensive. That single fact dispels the excuse that this type of design is a luxury for our cities.
The global standard for managing overwhelming stormwater is moving away from rapid channelization and toward the creation of temporary flood spaces. In highly dense urban environments like Rotterdam, architects have pioneered the concept of water squares .
These are sunken public plazas that function as basketball courts, skate parks, or open-air amphitheaters during the dry months. When a heavy rainfall hits, they are transformed into massive, safe water retention basins until the city's drains can cope, then releasing it.
For Bangladesh, this idea can be adapted without the high maintenance costs of European-style public spaces. Imagine a school playground in Mirpur, a stadium bowl, or a neglected field in Chittagong, each built slightly lower than the surrounding streets.
Most of the year, they remain what they are: Places to play. But on the few days when heavy rain arrives, the surrounding roads can be graded so water flows into them by gravity rather than into shops and homes.
There is no pump to fail or imported parts to replace. Once the rain stops and the drains clear, the temporary pond drains away, and the children return. Accepting that a few designated places will flood is far more practical than pretending our streets will not.
Singapore's celebrated transformation of the Kallang River from a plain concrete drainage channel into a naturalized, winding waterway offers a compelling visual of ecological urbanism. However, our reality involves a vastly different socio-economic landscape, primarily defined by heavy solid waste pollution and informal settlements.
For 30 years, our answer to a filthy canal has been to roof it over into a box culvert and stop looking at it, which simply hides the silt until it hardens into a plug no crew can reach without breaking the road above.
The better path would have been the opposite, to break those concrete lids and daylight the channels back into open water. Researchers mapped this for Dhaka's Begunbari canal , but past attempts prove daylighting alone fails.
Hatirjheel was meant to be Dhaka’s Bishan , a decaying canal system reborn as a wide lake in the heart of the capital. Late last year it won a major international award. In the same season, the people staying beside it were holding their noses, because the lake had become a sewage pond.
Its treatment chemicals exhausted earlier and a waterbody the size of a small town is maintained by a handful of workers. The idea was not wrong, but the sequence was. The lake was opened before stopping the sewage flow into it, so it was already being poisoned on inauguration day.
When Seoul uncovered its own celebrated stream downtown, it refused that mistake and treated the removal of sewage as a precondition of the project, laying pipes to carry the district's waste away first. The result today is a green ribbon that cools the streets around it . Seoul cleaned the water, then reopened it. We reopened ours, then let it rot.
A daylighted canal will work only if cleaning is built into its design from day one. To prevent these canals from becoming open sewers again, we also need to make better use of one of our most overlooked urban resources: The informal waste economy.
Instead of relying only on municipal cleaning crews, the canals could be designed with simple trash traps, floating barriers, and accessible collection points. Informal waste pickers could then have safe and structured access to these points, helping remove plastics and other waste before they cause blockages.
Native wetland plants along the canal banks could further stabilize the soil, reduce erosion, and filter some surface pollutants. Together, these measures can reduce the pressure on already stretched municipal budgets.
In Singapore, water quality is supported by designed wetlands and natural filtration. In Bangladesh, we could also harness the people already working within our informal waste economy, giving them a safer and more productive role in keeping our waterways clear.
A significant but rarely discussed driver of our drainage crisis is the burden that unchecked private development places on public infrastructure.
Every new commercial high-rise or apartment block that covers its plot with concrete sends more rainwater into already overwhelmed streets and drains.
The solution is to make large developments manage more of their own runoff. Building codes could require blue roofs that temporarily store rainwater and release it slowly, along with underground cisterns to collect water for flushing, cooling, and irrigation.
This would reduce the pressure on struggling, underfunded city corporations and make private developers share the cost of the urban growth from which they profit.
Portland's breakthrough came from embracing the power of the small. The American city once struggled with severe storm overflows that dumped raw sewage into its riverways. Rather than building a massive infrastructure, Portland paid ordinary citizens to disconnect 56,000 rooftop downspouts from the municipal sewers.
By letting rainwater absorb into private gardens, the city diverted over a billion gallons a year from its overloaded network. This approach endures because it lacks mechanical complexity. In a country like Bangladesh where centralized machinery is often the first to fail and the last to be repaired, this decentralized simplicity is worth more than any monument.
Every one of these ideas runs, in the end, onto the same reef that wrecked Hatirjheel, our national habit of celebration with grand inauguration ceremonies, only to be abandoned to long-term neglect.
To break this cycle, we must look backward to traditional practices. Historically, the maintenance of local water bodies, ponds, and drainage channels was a communal responsibility, deeply embedded in the civic fabric of rural life.
As millions migrated to the cities, this intrinsic stewardship was completely outsourced to a faceless, sprawling bureaucracy, leading to widespread apathy and a disconnect between citizens and their immediate environment.
We should be able to revive this stewardship by formalizing community guardianship over neighborhood drainage networks. Instead of awarding massive maintenance contracts to distant corporate entities who have no stake in the community's well-being, city authorities could issue decentralized micro-contracts.
These contracts would be awarded to local neighbourhood cooperatives, youth groups, or even organized associations within the informal settlements situated directly alongside the water bodies.
Paying the local community a steady wage to maintain the flow and cleanliness of their own immediate drainage channels ensures continuous, hyper- localized oversight.
Surviving the harsh, changing realities of our rain-battered delta requires abandoning the idea that engineering alone can control water. We cannot concrete our way out of the monsoon, nor can we simply rely on importing green infrastructure designed for very different climates.
The goal is not to become Singapore, Rotterdam, or Seoul. Their climate is different from ours, their resources are greater, and their institutions work differently. But they offer an important lesson: Water does not always have to be pushed away.
Cities can be designed to hold it, slow it down, and let it pass. The challenge for Bangladesh is to find ways to apply that principle to our own climate, resources, and realities.
The rain will fall again. Shopkeepers in Shantinagar and many other parts of the country will once again move their goods to higher shelves, just as they have done for years. We cannot stop the rain. But we can decide what happens when it falls.
Somewhere in this city, a dead, black canal could, within a few years, become a clean waterway where children play beside the water and families sit on the bank on a pleasant evening.
Dr Sabbir Ahmad, a tech executive with global experience in digital connectivity, sustainable infrastructure and energy, now shaping Bangladesh's semiconductor landscape as the CEO of Silicon Array Ltd. Email: sabbir@ieee.org.

item.title: The second wheel Bangladesh keeps ignoring. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On factory floors across Bangladesh right now, workers are welding frames that will never touch a sewing machine. What leaves those gates does not stitch anyone a shirt. It rolls out on two wheels, bound for Hamburg or Vienna. Nobody outside the industry notices them much. Perhaps they should.
Bangladesh's economy still speaks one language to the world. Garments alone brought in 84% of the country's export earnings last fiscal year , according to figures the commerce minister placed before parliament this June. A nation of 170 million people has built its entire trading identity around a needle and thread. That comfort has served us for four decades. It will not serve us for the next one.
There is a smaller story here that sits quietly beside the big one that needs a closer look. Quite remarkably, Bangladesh made a handsome $ 116.44 million from bicycle exports in fiscal year 2024/25 . This is a skyrocketed figure with a jump of 4% over the year before . Germany alone bought $34.39m worth of Bangladeshi bicycles. Eurostat now places Bangladesh as the third largest bicycle supplier to the European Union and the eighth largest in the world.
What makes the recovery worth watching is how it happened. Exports had touched $ 168m during the pandemic cycling rush , then fell by half once European retailers worked through their overstock and the war in Ukraine cooled demand further.
Plenty of export sectors never climb back after a fall like that. Bangladesh's bicycle makers did climb back, and that says more about the industry's staying power than any single good year could.
Europe is also moving in a direction that suits us. The European Cyclists' Federation expects the continent to sell 30 million bicycles a year by 2030 , close to 10 million more than today, driven by city planners redesigning streets and younger buyers choosing bikes over cars, not because of fashion.
There is a policy tailwind working in our favour too. The European Commission renewed its anti-dumping duties on Chinese bicycles in January 2025, this time extending the measure to cover electric bicycles as well . Brussels did more for Bangladeshi exporters with that single decision than most of our domestic industrial policy combined.
Here is where the celebration needs a pause. Protections handed down by someone else's trade ruling are never permanent. They come up for review.
Politics in Brussels can shift. And a much larger deadline is already bearing down on us. Bangladesh was to graduate from least developed country status on November 24, 2026 , though the government has now asked the United Nations to push that date to 2029 .
Whichever date holds, the World Trade Organization has warned Bangladesh could lose close to $8bn a year in export earnings once current trade preferences run out, while UNCTAD's own estimate runs as high as $17.5bn.
Most of that exposure sits with garments. It should still worry the bicycle industry, because a weakness sits right at its centre that nobody has fixed.
Bangladesh still imports the bulk of the expensive parts that go into every bicycle it exports. Annual demand for freewheels and sprockets alone runs to roughly 35 to 40 lakh and 50 to 55 lakh units, most of it met through imports, even though the Trade and Tariff Commission found local value addition in these parts already running close to 40% .
Every imported gear and chain raises our own production cost and sends the margin straight back to a foreign supplier. Garments could survive on imported fabric because labour was cheap enough to absorb the loss. Bicycles cannot lean on the same trick.
We have solved a version of this problem before. When motorcycle assemblers faced the identical bottleneck a decade ago, the government cut the duty on completely knocked down units by 25 percentage points in 2016 .
Within a few years, local manufacturing and assembly met 96% of domestic motorcycle demand instead of relying on imports for nearly all of it. Nobody had to invent a new economic model. A tariff structure changed, and investors responded.
The same tools sit within reach for bicycles. Lower duties on components would encourage local vendors to enter the space rather than depend on imports. Bonded warehouse access, already extended to garment factories, could be widened to cover bicycle component manufacturers as well.
Trade diplomacy with Brussels needs to begin now, while the graduation date is still being negotiated, not after the clock runs out and our negotiating position weakens.
Bangladesh has already shown twice that it can win foreign buyers on quality rather than cheap labour alone. Garments proved it first. Bicycles are proving it again, on a smaller scale but a genuine one.
The choice in front of us is whether we treat this as a pleasant accident or as a pillar our economy has needed since long before anyone in Frankfurt noticed our welders.
We built one industry because building two felt unnecessary. That comfort is running out of road faster than we think. Bicycles alone will not carry an economy of 170 million people. But they are proof that we can compete on something other than a sewing machine, provided we invest in the parts before the deadline arrives, not after.
Nazma Sultana holds a key strategic position at Akij Bicycle & Engineering Limited (ABEL).

item.title: The missing gratitude for thankless jobs. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The desk lamp in a newsroom in Dhaka flickers at 2:00 AM, casting long, fatigued shadows across pages of investigative drafts, while a weary educator in a rural government primary school in Kurigram corrects her 400th exam paper by the dim glow of a mobile phone torch.
Down the street, a municipal sanitation worker clears choked drains before dawn, unseen and unacknowledged by the waking city.
In the architecture of modern civilization, certain labour operates like the foundation of a building -- buried deep underground, taking the crushing weight of the entire structure, yet entirely forgotten until something breaks.
These are the thankless jobs.
Within the specific and high-stakes context of Bangladesh, the phrase "thankless job" takes on a sharp, almost harrowing edge.
To understand what truly constitutes a thankless job, we must look beyond the mere absence of praise.
A genuinely thankless job is defined by a paradox: Its practitioners bear the immense burden of sustaining societal truth, social mobility, and public health, yet they are systematically met with suspicion, ridicule, intimidation, and prosecution at whim.
What makes a job truly thankless? It is not merely low pay -- though financial precarity is almost always a faithful companion. Rather, it is the fundamental asymmetry between the liability one carries and the dignity one is afforded.
The journalist: Walking a tightrope of peril
Consider the journalist, particularly within the sociopolitical landscape of Bangladesh.
Journalism is ostensibly framed as the "fourth estate," a pillar of democracy. In reality, practicing independent journalism here often feels like walking a tightrope over an active volcano.
When a reporter uncovers systemic corruption in public procurement, financial sector anomalies, or bureaucratic inertia, the immediate reaction from the powerful is rarely introspection or reform.
Instead, it is a knee-jerk defense mechanism characterized by hostility. Journalists are routinely questioned, ridiculed in public forums, intimidated by non-state actors, and prosecuted under draconian legal instruments -- such as legacy cyber-security or digital safety laws that weaponize ambiguity against the press.
The public consumes the news with morning tea, often criticizing the media for being "biased" or "sensationalist," while remaining entirely insulated from the physical threats, midnight summons, and psychological toll borne by reporters in district towns and metropolitan hubs alike.
The journalist labours under a relentless cloud of hostility, where doing the job correctly makes you an enemy of those you hold accountable.
The frontline pillars
This dynamic extends far beyond the newsroom.
A thankless job, therefore, is one where society demands perfection, absorbs the immense value produced, and repays the worker with vulnerability, disrespect, and peril.
Why thankless jobs are the cogs of societal survival
It is easy to dismiss these professions as unfortunate casualties of economic inequality.
However, a deeper sociological examination reveals a chilling truth: Society runs smoothly precisely because these jobs are thankless.
The structural thanklessness of these roles is often the mechanism by which power dynamics are maintained and societal friction is absorbed. Without them, the veneer of order collapses.
To understand why the thankless job of the journalist is non-negotiable for a functioning society, we can look at a journalistic anecdote.
In the early 2020s, local investigative reports in regional Bangladeshi newspapers highlighted how syndicates were artificially inflating prices of essential commodities at local haats (traditional markets) through cartelization.
The journalists who broke these stories faced intense local pressure, threats of physical assault from local political muscle, and frivolous defamation lawsuits designed to bankrupt them legally.
Why did powerful vested interests react with such venom? Because journalism acts as society’s immune system.
When a pathogen (corruption, abuse of power, systemic theft) enters the body politic, the immune system attacks it. This process is inherently inflammatory and painful.
If journalists were thanked, coddled, and protected by the establishment, it would mean the establishment welcomed self-correction. But power rarely welcomes correction.
By making journalism thankless, a society attempts to suppress its own immune response.
Yet, without that painful, thankless reporting, the socioeconomic body rots from within.
Unchecked corruption drains national reserves, banking sectors hollow out, and inflation crushes the working class.
The journalist's thankless persistence is the only barrier preventing total systemic opacity.
Similarly, the thankless labour of the teacher is the glue holding social mobility together. In a developing economy like Bangladesh, education is the primary elevator out of intergenerational poverty.
When teachers in under-resourced classrooms dedicate their evenings to counseling struggling students or managing massive administrative burdens without adequate support, they are quietly absorbing the failures of the state's social welfare apparatus.
If teaching were truly valued and supported commensurate with its actual impact, resource allocation would shift dramatically.
By keeping the profession underpaid, overworked, and structurally unappreciated, the system manages to extract maximum emotional and intellectual labour at minimal cost -- treating educators as martyrs of necessity rather than professionals of value.
The Bangladeshi context and the path forward
In Bangladesh, the cultural narrative surrounding labour is often tied to visible, tangible production -- garments manufactured, bridges built, remittances sent from the Middle East.
These are celebrated, and rightly so; they drive the macroeconomic indicators.
However, the invisible labour -- the journalistic truth-telling, the foundational teaching, the municipal sanitation -- operates in the cultural blind spot.
We celebrate the ribbon-cuttings of mega-infrastructure projects, but we rarely protect or thank the journalists who investigate the structural integrity of those projects, nor the low-tier engineers and supervisors who blow the whistle on substandard materials at personal risk.
When we punish or ignore those in thankless jobs, we induce a profound societal brain drain and moral apathy.
Talented youth steer clear of investigative journalism, public school teaching, and civil rights advocacy, preferring safer, more lucrative corporate or bureaucratic tracks where compliance is rewarded over conscience.
A society that consumes the fruits of a thankless job while starving, intimidating, or prosecuting the tree-tender is borrowing prosperity from its own future.
True reform in Bangladesh requires a cultural and structural pivot. It demands legal safeguards that protect journalists from arbitrary prosecution, fair compensation and social prestige for educators, and basic human dignity for frontline workers.
Until we recognize that the health of a nation is measured not just by its tall buildings and export volumes, but by how it treats those who bear its heaviest and most unrewarded crosses, our progress will remain fragile -- built on the exhausted backs of those we refuse to thank.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on Sunday released left-arm wrist spinner Sufiyan Moqim from the national men’s squad for the ongoing One-day International tri-series involving England and Sri Lanka, citing the nature of the pitches in Lahore, while adding left-handed batter Maaz Sadaqat as cover for players carrying minor niggles.

In a brief statement, the PCB said Sufiyan had been released from the squad “keeping in view the nature of Lahore pitches” and would return to domestic cricket. Maaz, meanwhile, had been added as cover for players with minor niggles.

The move comes as the tri-series shifts to the Gaddafi Stadium after the opening three matches in Rawalpindi. Pakistan have won both their league games so far, beating Sri Lanka by 37 runs and England by 87, and face England again in Lahore on Sunday. The pitches in Rawalpindi generally favoured pace, limiting opportunities for specialist spinners.

Sufiyan, who hails from Azad Kashmir, has represented Pakistan in limited-overs cricket since making his T20I debut in 2023. He is best known for his record-equalling figures of five for three against Zimbabwe in a T20 International and was named Player of the Tournament in the 2026 Pakistan Super League while playing for Peshawar Zalmi. In ODIs, he has taken eight wickets in four matches.

Maaz, 21, has attracted attention with his aggressive batting. The Peshawar-born left-hander made an immediate impact on his ODI debut against Bangladesh earlier this year and recently impressed in the T20I series against Sri Lanka, scoring consecutive half-centuries, including a blistering 96 off 51 balls that helped Pakistan post their highest T20I total at home.

An occasional left-arm orthodox spinner, Maaz had initially been left out of the tri-series squad.

The updated squad, led by Shaheen Shah Afridi, now includes Maaz as Pakistan continue their campaign in Lahore ahead of the final on Oct 31 at the same venue.

item.title: Where is the justice?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There's an old saying that all of economics is either footnotes to Adam Smith or wrong.
Like most old sayings, it's not wholly and exactly correct but there is still a great deal of truth in it.
For one of the reasons that old sayings survive is that people note there's a lot of truth in there and so keep repeating it.
That we've still got the saying can thus be a proof that there's a useful amount of truth in it.
With that in mind, we can discuss the disaster that is this news : “Bangladesh ranked 123rd among 143 countries and jurisdictions in the World Justice Project (WJP) index” and justice here is referring to things like corruption, regulatory enforcement, and so on, eight areas in total.
The one that concerns us here is “civil justice was the second-weakest area, with Bangladesh ranking 132nd and scoring 0.36.”
We know about corruption, about the ineffectiveness of regulatory enforcement, and so on. But thieves and incompetence we also don't want. The effectiveness -- or not -- of civil justice is one of those things not enough people think about enough of the time.
Adam Smith did point out that “little else is requisite to carry a state to the highest degree of opulence from the lowest barbarism but peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice: All the rest being brought about by the natural course of things.”
Peace we're all doing pretty well on in this corner of the world. Easy taxes could be easier but the Bangladeshi state does not swallow an inordinate amount of everyone's production or work.
Which leaves us that administration of justice.
Given that we are talking about the economy here, it's that part of justice associated with the economy that matters to us.
The ability to go to court and get as the contract enforced -- say. Which is, as we know, a wholly laughable proposition in the Bangladeshi courts of today. Which is, therefore, the thing that needs to be fixed.
We can also borrow something from our other ideas about the economy. That, in business at least, it is often better to make a fast decision than delay and then, perhaps, make the right one.
Borrowing that idea means that the law, about contracts and commerce, needs to be fast. It's better that it be fast than it be wholly just or near perfect.
A decision -- even, sometimes the wrong one -- given now is better than grinding through the process for another five years.
Something that will be anathema to the lawyers of course, they get paid by the hour, but still true all the same.
It would be even better if we always got the right decisions -- but let's do this step by step. We need commercial law -- that part of civil justice which works with business and the economy -- to be swift.
We also need it to be certain. If the contract says something, it must be definitive. The same is true for the law -- that's what the decision will be.
Those decisions need to come quickly. These two conditions are more important than grinding through to a decision in a decade.
It's not wholly true that Adam Smith was correct about everything he discussed but it's still a remarkably good basis to start our reasoning from. As he points out, there are things that governments really do have to do in order to ensure that the economy grows.
One of these is a commercial legal system that actually works. And by works, we mean swift and certain decisions more than necessarily wholly fair or even correct ones.
As the World Justice Project's index points out, this is something Bangladesh is failing upon and failing badly. We should correct that error.
We all know that it's going to take years, if not decades, to recover the money from those who looted the banks last decade. If nothing else about efficient justice, it would be nice to bankrupt the thieves before they die, no? You know, the tolerable administration of justice.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Weaponizing humiliation. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Perhaps there is no such thing as privacy in Bangladesh. Even where it exists, many in the authorities or the media do not understand what it means. Even if they do understand, they are unwilling to act according to the essence of privacy.
This unwillingness is strongest when an opportunity arises to violate a woman’s privacy. Society has still not found any way to suppress the urge to humiliate women in public.
Last Tuesday, personnel of the detective branch raided the residence of an Additional DIG of police in Purbachal, near Dhaka. It was described as an anti-narcotics operation (though these days even a raid on a club or bar is called an “anti-narcotics operation”). But there did not seem to be much presence of drugs there.
In the photos released, although there was a bottle and a half of liquor, the absence of narcotics was noticeable. However, that is not the problem with this operation. The question is about the way the operation was publicized in the media, or the way arrangements were made to publicize it.
Some days ago, during a police raid on a club called German Club in Dhaka, the entire scene was being filmed from outside the main gate. As the club’s guests came out one by one, they were filmed, and the video was spread on social media, with one particular woman going viral on social media.
But what happened in Purbachal was even more disgraceful, and here it was not only the unbridled content creators of social media, but even established mainstream news media that got involved.
Videos were shot inside the Purbachal house, in various rooms. When several girls came down the stairs from the upper floor, one or two tried to cover their faces with their orna (scarf) while their faces were being filmed, but most could not.
The men present also appeared in the video, though the focus was mostly on the women. Hearing the description of the raid, many will assume that some “immoral activity” was going on there. And when, on top of that, one woman’s face after another appears in the video, no psychologist is needed to understand what picture forms in the public’s mind.
Here the question may be asked: Which is the immoral activity? Adult men and women socializing inside a home? Or is it the filming of women, calling the house a “harem,” and humiliating them socially?
By shooting and circulating the video, the women were not merely humiliated. They were humiliated knowingly and deliberately, and their safety was put at risk.
One thing needs to be made clear. It is normal for police to record videos in any operation. It is important to preserve through video information such as whether the operation is being conducted according to the police’s own rules, how and where evidence was found, and how and where the detainees were held.
But that video would be the police’s own evidence, meant to assist their own investigation, an important part of the process of collecting testimony and evidence against the accused.
Such a video will play an important role in framing formal charges and conducting the case. Similarly, the accused’s lawyers can use these same police videos to try to get the allegations against their client dismissed. But the videos of the recent operations do not seem to have been taken to assist a case.
First, it is not clear who shot the videos. At least from the video taken outside the gate of German Club, it seemed that it was no one from the police. That is, someone who got news of the raid went there and filmed it.
Is the Purbachal incident the same? The videos were taken both inside and outside the house. One woman was seen pointing a finger at the person filming and saying something. Had someone from the police been holding the camera, that woman would perhaps not have done so.
The most disgraceful thing was spreading those videos on social media, exposing the women’s faces, and humiliating them in public.
Such an incident, while not common, once again begs the question of ethics in a section of the country’s media. Law enforcement agencies also have a big role in building this habit.
For many years, the police, and later RAB or BGB, have been supplying the media with photos and identities of people detained on charges of some alleged crime.
Even when the detainee was only a suspect, his photo was given to the media, often with a signboard calling him a criminal hung around his neck. This still happens.
That a person is innocent until proven guilty in court, this fundamental principle of law seems to be unknown to Bangladesh’s law enforcement agencies.
The Bangladeshi media industry too has never quite had anything in the way of editorial policy or ethical standards. Some large organizations have discussed ethics and, in some cases, tried to create a policy of their own.
For example, at one time the photos and identities of women who were victims of rape used to be printed. But that has changed. The identity of victims is now kept secret in most cases.
But the accused also deserve this kind of protection. Formal charges can be framed against someone only when there is sufficient evidence, and until charges are framed, the identity of the accused should also be kept secret.
Even now, photos of accused or suspected persons provided by the police are being published along with their identities. As for social media content creators, that is a separate matter, and it is doubtful whether there is any editorial vetting in their work.
In many cases, such creators run a channel single-handedly, and they depend entirely on view counts and engagement for income. They do not have time to worry about editorial “decency” or ethical considerations.
Established mainstream media is a different matter. They have staff and the capacity to read and think about what has been done in other countries of the world on journalistic rules, editorial policy, ethics, and so on.
It is possible for them to create their own policies on how to report while protecting the rights, privacy, and safety of ordinary people, and to give journalists the necessary training on these matters.
In particular, established media can sensitize journalists on how to cover delicate stories involving women, children, religious or ethnic minorities, and other vulnerable groups.
This work should have been done long ago. But even now, photos, names, and identities of detainees provided by the police are still being published.
The media needs to think about how their reporting can harm ordinary people. Care must be taken so that people who are innocent in the eyes of the law are not declared “guilty” in a media trial and socially humiliated.
Humiliating those who have no power, who are not wealthy, who have no connections in high circles, and who have no influential mama-chacha in political circles is not merely wrong. It is quite literally another crime. This is especially so when women’s photos or videos are being published with no regard for their social dignity and safety.
Just as initiative is needed from the media industry to stop this practice, the government also needs to impose restrictions on the police so that they do not do anything that could humiliate people before a trial in court.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Nothing is more important than protecting our children. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The recurring reports of physical and sexual abuse of children within educational institutions across the country lay bare what can only be termed a horrifying national failure.
When schools, madrasas, and learning centres - places meant to nurture and protect our nation’s youth - become sites of predatory violence and terror, the foundational contract between society and the state is shattered.
Recent alarms raised by child rights advocates regarding abuse cases expose a pervasive, systemic rot that can no longer be ignored or swept under the rug with bureaucratic platitudes.
For too long, child protection in Bangladesh has been undermined by a culture of silence, social stigma, and institutional cover-ups. Predators are allowed to operate with virtual impunity, exploiting power imbalances to silence vulnerable victims through threats and intimidation.
When children are forced to choose between their education and their personal safety, the institutional framework entrusted with their welfare has utterly collapsed.
Protecting children cannot remain a rhetorical talking point for NGOs and press releases. The government must immediately enforce rigorous, binding child-protection protocols across every educational institution nationwide, without exception.
Allegations of abuse must be met with swift, impartial criminal investigation, prosecution, and absolute accountability, stripping away the impunity enjoyed by so many perpetrators.
Educational authorities too must do their part by establishing secure, confidential reporting channels and robust psychosocial support systems, ensuring that victims and their families are believed, protected, and prioritized.
A nation that fails to safeguard its children from predators within its own classrooms has forfeited its moral authority. We need to be getting rid of this rot with the urgency it warrants, ruthlessly purging abusive environments and transforming our schools and madrasas into genuine safe havens before more generations of children are scarred by institutional cowardice.

item.title: Logistical deficits not a good enough excuse for law enforcement. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There is no denying the grueling realities faced by ground-level law enforcement personnel in Bangladesh.
It cannot be easy to operate amid severe logistical deficits, including acute transport shortages and a lack of proper housing facilities, for nearly 90% of the force. Officers also often endure grueling 12-to-16-hour shifts under immense pressure.
This is a reality we must acknowledge, and we sympathize with those within the forces.
Equipping the force with necessary transport, housing, and operational backing is thus a vital administrative duty that the government must address without delay.
However, recognizing the genuine hardships of police work must never translate into a blanket excuse for systemic failure or poor public service.
The primary grievance of ordinary citizens with law enforcement agencies has been an entrenched culture of authoritarian intimidation and a callous disregard for public welfare.
Too often, the badge has been wielded as an instrument of power and coercion rather than protection, leaving communities alienated and terrified of the very institutions meant to secure them.
Logistical upgrades and multi-crore vehicle procurements will mean nothing if the internal ethos of the force remains rot-ridden.
A lack of transport does not excuse extortion at checkpoints, nor does substandard housing justify custodial abuse, bribery, or the routine weaponization of the law against the vulnerable.
For generations, citizens have been forced to navigate a police apparatus that views them with suspicion or contempt rather than dignity and service. For that to change, it will take more than overhauling institutional capacity.
Accountability must match investment step for step. Officers deserve fair working conditions and adequate resources, but the public deserves law enforcement agencies that genuinely care for and protect them.

item.title: Aurangzeb rules out consumption-led growth, says tariff reforms will continue. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb has ruled out pursuing liquidity-fuelled, consumption-led economic growth, saying Pakistan must prioritise sustainable, export-led expansion and continue with tariff reforms to improve the competitiveness of its industries.

Speaking at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (Lums) on Saturday, Aurangzeb said Pakistan could not afford to repeat the cycle of import-dependent growth that had previously led to balance-of-payments problems and forced the country to seek support from lenders of last resort.

He said the government was committed to continuing tariff reforms, primarily to reduce the cost of raw materials and intermediate goods for exporters, despite concerns over the timing of the measures.

“We are very clear: no matter how much pressure there is, we are not going to go for liquidity-fuelled, consumption-led growth,” he said, adding that Pakistan needed to avoid another cycle in which a temporary acceleration in economic activity was followed by a balance-of-payments crisis.

Aurangzeb said the government had attempted to provide a direction towards export-led growth in the latest budget through measures including the elimination of super taxes, reductions in tax slabs and financing for exporters at 4.5 per cent.

On tariff reforms, he said the government had protected domestic industries for too long without sunset clauses and that the existing approach could not continue indefinitely.

“We are in year two of the tariff reform, and we are going to continue with that; there is no turning back,” he said.

The finance minister also stressed that economic growth needed to generate employment, pointing to the contrast between Pakistan’s growth trajectory and that of its neighbour, where growth of 7 to 8pc, he argued, had not translated into sufficient job creation.

“That’s why you see people there where they are,” he said, emphasising that the sectors driving growth must also address unemployment.

Global outlook remains uncertain

Reflecting on discussions at international forums in New York, London and Bangkok ahead of the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Aurangzeb said the global economy had remained resilient but faced an uncertain and worrying outlook.

He identified growing differences in economic fortunes between oil-exporting and oil-importing countries, as well as economies benefiting from artificial intelligence, as key themes in discussions on global growth.

Energy shocks and the El Nino weather phenomenon had featured prominently in discussions, he said, warning that their effects were intensifying and contributing to food-security concerns in some parts of the world.

He also highlighted high debt levels, limited fiscal space in some economies and the growing importance of digital infrastructure and labour-market preparedness for artificial intelligence.

As trade fragmentation and geopolitical polarisation intensified, regional corridors and regional blocs were emerging as significant opportunities, he said, adding that these developments could be particularly important for Pakistan.

Twin deficits narrow

The finance czar said Pakistan had made significant progress in reducing its fiscal and external imbalances, with the combined twin deficits falling from 12.5pc of gross domestic product (GDP) to 2.6pc by the end of the last fiscal year.

He said the fiscal deficit had dropped to a 22-year low, while the country had recorded primary surpluses for three consecutive years. The current account deficit narrowed to around 0.1pc of GDP, supported by remittances and IT exports.

Aurangzeb said IT export services had risen from less than $1 billion to $4.6bn and were projected to reach $5.5bn in the current fiscal year. Foreign exchange reserves had improved to over three months of import cover, compared with two weeks during the crisis.

Citing three credit-rating upgrades since April last year, he said a recent Panda bond had attracted an order book twice its size, reflecting investor confidence beyond Pakistan’s current IMF programme, due to end in October next year.

Conflict puts pressure on energy security

He further said that Pakistan had managed immediate energy-supply challenges amid the continuing Middle East conflict, with supplies secured through November and arrangements for winter underway.

He said the government had shifted from blanket subsidies to targeted support, citing the high cost of universal subsidies.

Assuming an average household size of four to five people, the programme had reached an estimated 40 million to 50 million people, he said, adding that energy and gas supplies remained areas requiring attention.

Debt management and access to finance

The minister maintained that government borrowing had placed a disproportionate burden on the banking sector, but domestic debt-management operations had helped reduce debt-servicing costs to Rs6.9 trillion against a budgeted Rs8.2tr in the last fiscal year.

He said external debt payments had declined from $26.5 billion last year to $21.5bn in the current fiscal year and were expected to fall further. New external borrowing was largely aimed at replacing existing obligations, rather than increasing the debt burden.

Aurangzeb also highlighted pension reforms, saying new entrants to the civil bureaucracy had shifted from defined-benefit to defined-contribution schemes, while discussions with the armed forces were ongoing.

Population, investment and inclusive growth

The finance minister said the government has identified climate change and population growth as major challenges for Pakistan, urging measures to reduce the country’s 2.55pc population growth rate.

He cited Bangladesh, Indonesia and Iran as examples, saying all three had reduced their population growth rates to below 1pc over a decade. He stressed women’s education, workforce participation and engagement with religious scholars as key measures.

Aurangzeb said restoring investor confidence required macroeconomic stability and the clearance of around $4 billion in outstanding dividend and profit repatriation obligations.

He also highlighted improving domestic investment, citing 11 initial public offerings last year — a 20-year high — and five in the current year.

The finance minister said harmonising federal and provincial regulatory frameworks was essential to attract investment, as businesses often faced differing requirements at both levels. He stressed that reforms in taxation, energy and financing were necessary to sustain growth, improve export competitiveness and create jobs.

Measles: Beyond the blame game. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Official data from the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) recorded as of October 23, 2026, presents a heartbreaking reality for our nation: The combined measles death toll has reached 1,214 fatalities.
With nationwide suspected cases surging past 218,870 during the same reporting window, public anger and frustration are entirely justified.
When parents lose their children to a disease that is supposed to be fully preventable by routine immunization, asking hard questions is not just right, it is necessary.
If there has been institutional negligence, administrative complacency, or a lack of absolute sincerity in rolling out and monitoring proper vaccination coverage, those responsible must be held strictly accountable through transparent investigations and exemplary punishment.
Public trust in our national health programs depends on zero tolerance for official dereliction of duty.
Yet, while safeguarding vaccination integrity is our absolute first line of defense, fixing this crisis requires looking at the complete picture.
The frustration on the streets must be matched by a deeper understanding of the multi-layered vulnerabilities that allow this virus to devastate our communities.
To understand why this outbreak has taken such a devastating toll, we must examine who is being affected.
While the official DGHS divisional data shows that transmission spans all eight divisions, the outbreak burden is heavily concentrated in Dhaka and Chittagong, which together account for over 60% of nationwide cases and deaths, alongside significant mortality in Barisal, Sylhet, and Mymensingh.
Surveillance patterns and media reports point toward a clear socio-economic reality: The vast majority of severe hospitalizations and fatalities occur among children in congested urban slums, informal settlements, and hard-to-reach riverine regions.
These parents face grinding daily economic struggles and limited educational access, meaning missed routine Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) doses are often exacerbated by systemic barriers and logistical failures.
However, focusing solely on vaccination gaps misses a critical biological reality. Measles severity and mortality are intimately tied to a child's baseline nutritional status.
Persistent food inflation forces vulnerable families to cut back on high-quality animal proteins, such as eggs, milk, poultry, and meat which are essential for providing bioavailable iron, zinc, and Vitamin A.
A malnourished child possesses compromised cell-mediated immunity; when the measles virus strikes, their depleted defense systems fail to contain it, turning a manageable childhood infection into a fatal crisis.
For the children who survive the acute phase of measles, a hidden and insidious danger remains: "Immune amnesia."
Medical science demonstrates that the measles virus systematically wipes out a significant portion of the body's immune memory cells.
In the months and years following recovery, these children essentially "forget" how to fight off everyday bacterial and viral pathogens they previously resisted, leaving them perilously vulnerable to secondary infections.
Overcoming this requires structured post-recovery care, immediate Vitamin A supplementation, and sustained, protein-rich diets to help rebuild their shattered immune architecture.
Though measles is a human-to-human virus rather than a zoonotic pathogen, managing its threat effectively requires evaluating how broader environmental, agricultural, and socio-economic systems intersect with public health.
A One Health framework recognizes that human immunity and disease transmission do not exist in clinical isolation:
Toward collective action
If we are to prevent future tragedies and break the cycle of recurring health crises, we must combine unsparing accountability for vaccination delivery with comprehensive structural reform:
Measles is entirely preventable. The true measure of our public health resilience is not how many hospital beds we scramble to arrange during an emergency, but how strictly we enforce accountability, maintain flawless vaccination coverage, and protect our children through robust nutrition and an integrated defense.
Professor Dr KBM Saiful Islam is the former Dean of the Faculty of Animal Science & Veterinary Medicine and former Chairman of the Department of Medicine & Public Health at Sher‑e‑Bangla Agricultural University. He previously served as a member of the National Coordination Committee of One Health Bangladesh.

item.title: The United Nations at 81: The world still waits for action. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On October 24 2026, the world observes “United Nations Day” amid a profound test of international cooperation. Wars threaten civilians, geopolitical rivalries obstruct collective action, human rights remain unevenly protected, and climate change disproportionately affects the most vulnerable.
Established in the aftermath of WWII, the United Nations (UN) embodied a historic ambition: To prevent future conflicts through dialogue, diplomacy and collective action.
Eighty-one years after its Charter entered into force, that ambition remains indispensable. Yet, the widening gap between its founding ideals and present realities raises a critical question: Can the UN still deliver on its promise?
Although every member state has an equal vote in the General Assembly, influence remains unequal, particularly in the Security Council. The challenge is not whether the world needs the UN, but whether it can become more effective, representative, and accountable.
The Security Council’s ability to act decisively is frequently constrained by geopolitical rivalries and the veto power of its five permanent members. When strategic interests prevail over collective responsibility, the credibility of the international system suffers -- and civilians pay the price. Families lose their homes, children are deprived of education, and millions are forced to flee.
Peace must mean more than the absence of fighting. It must allow people to return home safely, live without fear, and rebuild their lives with dignity.
Greater representation for underrepresented regions and meaningful restraint in the use of the veto when mass atrocities occur would strengthen the organization’s legitimacy. Such reforms, however, require genuine political will from influential member states.
Rebuilding trust in multilateralism
Rising nationalism, political polarization, and declining public confidence are straining international cooperation. Some governments view international agreements as constraints on sovereignty, while others question whether multilateral institutions apply their principles consistently.
Restoring trust requires fairness, transparency, and measurable results. Powerful nations must accept the same accountability they demand of others.
These divisions were evident during the 81st session of the General Assembly. On September 23, Argentine President Javier Milei described the UN as an “ineffective organization” and its officials as “arrogant parasites.” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, by contrast, called for Security Council reform and the abolition of the veto.
Restrictions driven by political considerations can undermine humanitarian assistance and essential services. The answer is not weaker multilateralism, but more credible and dependable cooperation, supported by transparency and honoured commitments.
Pandemics, climate change, and cyber threats demonstrate that no country can adequately address major global challenges alone. Responsible multilateralism serves national interests as well as humanity’s shared interests.
Human rights must be universal
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights established a common standard of dignity, freedom, and equality. Yet its principles remain unevenly upheld.
Governments sometimes invoke sovereignty to deflect criticism, while surveillance, online censorship, and digital repression create new threats to fundamental freedoms.
The UN’s credibility depends on defending human rights consistently, without political selectivity. Civilian protection, freedom of expression, and equality before the law must never become bargaining chips in geopolitical alliances.
Credible investigations and accountability for serious violations are essential to ensuring that justice does not depend on political influence.
Sustainable development requires global solidarity
The 2030 Agenda and its 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) provide a shared framework for tackling poverty, inequality, inadequate healthcare, educational disparities, and environmental degradation. Yet, economic shocks, debt distress, and climate change continue to obstruct progress.
Communities that have contributed least to environmental pressures often possess the fewest resources to withstand their consequences.
For Bangladesh, international cooperation is vital to securing affordable and predictable climate finance, accessible technology, capacity-building, and fairer economic arrangements.
Reforming the global financial architecture and addressing unsustainable debt must remain priorities. Wealthier nations must also translate their climate commitments into tangible action.
Nevertheless, international assistance alone cannot guarantee development. Effective national leadership, sound governance, and accountability are equally important.
The UN should support national priorities while ensuring that development reaches communities most at risk of being left behind.
The 81st session’s priority theme, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all,” captures the challenge. Trust must be earned through tangible improvements in people’s lives. The UN needs stronger coordination among its agencies and greater accountability for results.
Responsibility is shared. An organization established by governments cannot overcome international divisions without their cooperation. Civil society, young people, and journalists also play vital roles in holding institutions accountable and translating global commitments into local action.
Bangladesh and other developing countries should build coalitions, advocate fairer international rules, and ensure that vulnerable communities have a meaningful voice in global decision-making.
A renewed commitment
This day should prompt reflection on the distance between the world we aspire to build and the realities people experience.
The UN is far from perfect, but the need for a forum where nations can negotiate and cooperate remains undeniable. As UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih stated, “Peace must be measured not only by agreements signed, but by lives changed.”
At 81, the UN needs renewed commitment to its founding principles, meaningful institutional reform, and a willingness among member states to place humanity above narrow political interests.
Its success must be measured not by the resolutions it adopts, but by its ability to alleviate the suffering caused by war, protect human rights, expand opportunities for developing countries, and safeguard the planet for future generations.
The world needs a United Nations that does more than speak on behalf of all; it needs one that delivers for all.
Nicholas Biswas , is a media freelancer and recipient of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) Media Award.

item.title: Sharing the streets. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bringing Dhaka’s street food vendors under a formal registration system -- through the Bangladesh Safe Food Authority initiative starting on November 1 -- is a reasonable step towards improving food safety and recognizing a sector that has long operated informally.
While the authorities prepare to introduce mandatory registration, however, they must also ensure that the process offers vendors genuine protection rather than another reason for them to fear harassment.
The initiative has the potential to make food safety oversight more effective for both traders and consumers by identifying vendors, providing hygiene training, and establishing clear standards. Free initial registration is also a welcome decision, particularly for people whose livelihoods depend on small daily earnings.
However, registration alone cannot address the difficulties street vendors face: Many continue to work under the threat of extortion and arbitrary eviction, often without access to designated spaces where they can operate without obstructing pedestrians.
A certificate will not amount to much if vendors remain vulnerable to illegal demands or are removed from their workplaces without clear rules or due process.
The authorities must therefore treat registration as part of a broader policy for managing street commerce. Local administrations need to establish designated vending areas, communicate regulations clearly, and ensure that enforcement is consistent and transparent. Vendors should also be made aware of necessary documentation, expected standards, and clear, formal ways to report harassment.
At the same time, food safety cannot be treated as a mere formality. Vendors should receive practical guidance and reasonable opportunities to meet hygiene requirements, while those who repeatedly disregard essential standards are held accountable.
Dhaka needs cleaner, safer, and better-organized streets, but this cannot come at the cost of livelihoods without offering workable alternatives.
At the end of the day, whether this formal registration system is used to support compliance, protect small traders, and regulate public spaces fairly or simply add another layer of bureaucracy remains to be seen.

item.title: For meaningful transport overhaul. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
However, the real test of this initiative will be whether it leads to meaningful improvements in how buses operate, rather than remaining a cosmetic exercise.
For years, Dhaka’s commuters have endured overcrowding, reckless driving, competition for passengers, unsafe boarding and disembarking, and buses that are poorly maintained.
These problems cannot be solved through superficial changes alone. Even after these planned reforms, if buses continue to stop wherever their drivers please, compete dangerously with other vehicles, and disregard traffic rules, little will have changed for the people who depend on it every day.
This is not to dismiss the value of the initiative. Visible changes can help establish a new standard, and a phased approach may be more practical than attempting to overhaul the entire system overnight.
But such measures must be accompanied by stronger regulation, regular fitness inspections, disciplined route management, and consistent enforcement of traffic laws. Bus owners and operators must also be held accountable for the conduct of their drivers and the safety of their vehicles.
Equally important is improving the experience of passengers. Properly designated stops, safer boarding facilities, reliable services, and reasonable fares are essential to making public transport more dependable.
Workers in the sector must also be brought into the reform process, with clear rules and incentives that discourage reckless competition.
Dhaka cannot afford to keep revisiting the same problems through successive rounds of cosmetic change. The new colours can be a welcome first step, but they must mark the beginning of a sustained effort to reform public transport.
Ultimately, commuters need buses that are safe, reliable, and accountable -- not merely buses that look different.

item.title: Millions removed from India's draft voter rolls viewed as targeting of Muslims. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Millions removed from India's draft voter rolls viewed as targeting of Muslims

Submitted by Muheet Ul Islam on Fri, 10/23/2026 - 15:54
Over 100 million people have been removed from the voter list, and many are questioning why specific communities are overrepresented
A student activist holds a poster while on a bus after getting detained during a protest demanding the resignation of the nation's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter roll irregularities linked to the 'special intensive revision', in New Delhi on 13 October 2026 (Arun Sankar/AFP)
Off

Sameen Ud Din has lived at the same address in Old Delhi for years. He voted in the 2025 Delhi elections. But when the draft voter list for the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, was published this time around, his name was missing.

“It is an irony not to find my name in the SIR list. I did not receive any notice from the Election Commission of India [ECI] when my name was deleted,” Din, a 44-year-old businessman from the Nizam Ud Din area of Old Delhi, told Middle East Eye.

“I am now being asked to fill out Form 6, an application to register as a new voter, which is clearly a false declaration and carries penal consequences,” he added.

Din said he did not know what would happen next and felt pressured to submit the form. India's next general election is in 2029.

But Din is not alone. Muslims in different parts of India have reported similar problems, with countless people finding their names missing from the draft voter lists.

Approximately 133 million names had been flagged for removal from the voter list.

Critics say many eligible voters have been removed, with Muslims and Dalits – Dalits occupy the lowest rung in Hinduism’s caste system – among those mostly affected. 

An investigation from The Wire shows that in West Bengal, out of 2.75 million on the published list of removals, approximately 1.8 million were Muslims - or around 70 percent of the total published "ineligible to vote" list. Muslims make up just 25 percent of that state's electorate.

In some districts, according to The Wire, removals of Muslims made up over 90 percent of the total published removals.

This disparity has also brought protesters onto the streets of New Delhi. At one mid-October protest, India's Congress Party estimated that 250,000 people were present, while tens of thousands have been protesting across the country.

Protests suppressed

The Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP, called for demonstrations against the SIR under the slogan “Lehra Do Tiranga” or “Wave the Tricolour”. Protesters carrying national flags gathered at Connaught Place before moving towards Dilli Haat and other parts of central Delhi.

“Gyanesh Kumar, resign”, “Down with Delhi Police”, and “Whenever Modi is scared, he sends the police to the front” were among the other slogans protesters shouted.

'Our demand is clear: roll back the SIR because it is a state tool to change the country’s voting demographics'

- Vishnu, protester

The CJP began in May 2026 as a satirical online movement founded by digital strategist Abhijeet Dipke.

At the time, the movement was demanding the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, a senior leader of the Bharatiya Janata Party or BJP, and the education minister in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s cabinet. The protest came after the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET), one of the world’s largest medical entrance exams, was leaked; it determines admissions into five-year undergraduate medical courses in India.

It has since developed into a street protest movement.

Today protesters now want the government to stop the SIR and demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Figures cited by the ruling BJP show that about 130 million names were dropped from draft voter lists during the revision of the list. The ECI says the deletions are meant to clean up the rolls by removing the names of dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.

The protests against these actions took place despite a ban imposed by the BJP-led Delhi government on gatherings of four or more people in some areas. 

The restrictions came after Delhi Police removed Jantar Mantar, an 18th-century observatory and a long-time protest site, from its list of approved protest locations on 12 October. Police named Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi as alternative locations.

“We are out to protest to protect democracy. There is no violence going on, but the police are still detaining people. It is illegal. These detentions are a symbol of a fascist state, and this has been happening in India for a long time,” a protester who gave only his first name, Vishnu, told MEE.

He was speaking from a private vehicle hired by Delhi Police to transport detained protesters.

“Our demand is clear: roll back the SIR because it is a state tool to change the country’s voting demographics. They have done it successfully in many places, and we want people to join us and fight this fascist government with us,” he added.

Police detained several CJP leaders and protesters during the demonstrations, including Dipke and All India Students Association president, Neha Bora.

Bora was released on Saturday morning. Dipke appeared before a Special Executive Magistrate court and was released after signing a bond, according to reports. Delhi Police registered at least two cases over the march for violating prohibitory orders.

‘Deleted votes are those of Muslims’ 

On 23 September, The Indian Express published an investigation into alleged irregularities at the Election Commission. The report said the ECI had bypassed legal requirements, raised concerns over the SIR and centralised the voter database.

It also reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions and orders issued without their knowledge, approval or consultation. Their concerns included the addition and deletion of voters, changes to Form 6, access to the electoral database, and the commission’s technology systems.

The ECI rejected claims of an internal rift. It said the notes were suggestions and that every decision taken in the past year, including those related to the SIR, was unanimous. 

Where do Muslim youths fit in India's 'Cockroach' protests?
Read More »

For SIR critics, however, the concern goes beyond the Election Commission's functioning. They say the revisions could determine who can vote and, in turn, affect India’s political landscape. 

Ajay Gudavarthy, an associate professor at the Centre for Political Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi, said available data on voter deletions suggested that Muslims made up a large share of those removed from the rolls. 

He said he believed the deletions were part of a wider political strategy targeting Muslims and Dalits while building support among Other Backward Class, or OBCs, and upper castes. OBC is an official term employed by the government of India and is an umbrella classification for communities that are deprived or disadvantaged, whether economically, socially or in terms of education. 

“An overwhelming majority of the deleted votes are those of Muslims. This is one reason there is no mass outrage against the SIR. The BJP’s larger design is not only to delete Muslim votes but also to socially polarise people on the basis of these deletions,” Gudavarthy told MEE.

“Alongside Muslims, Dalit votes are also being deleted in order to achieve a reverse consolidation of OBCs and the upper castes,” he added.

The experience of Sayed Rashad Ikmal’s family in Odisha shows how the deletion of names can affect voters at the local level.

Ikmal, a resident of Sungra village in Cuttack district, said the names of his aunt and her husband were missing from the draft SIR voter list, even though his uncle had worked in the finance department of Indian Railways.

“The omission came as a shock to the family, which, like several others in the village, worried about being left off the voter rolls,” Ikmal told MEE.

The family approached the booth-level officer and found that a Form 7 application had been filed with the ECI seeking the deletion of their names. Form 7 is used to object to the inclusion of a name or request the removal of an existing name from the voter roll.

The family later approached the Block Development Officer [BDO], who cancelled the request and restored both names to the SIR list, Ikmal told MEE.

He said the BDO's role was important because local officials could prevent people from being wrongly removed from voter lists. 

India's 'Cockroach Party' takes aim at Narendra Modi's government after national exam debacle
Read More »

“If the BDO does his job honestly, wrongful additions to or deletions from the voter rolls can be stopped, whatever happens at the higher level,” he said.

The residents of Sungra and nearby villages, Ikmal said, had begun to feel that Muslims were being targeted in Odisha. He said these concerns had grown alongside the spread of the “Go to Bangladesh” narrative among people linked to Hindu right-wing groups.

“I describe the threat of being sent to Bangladesh as one of the most intimidating narratives directed at Muslims,” Ikmal said, referring to political claims about Bangladeshi infiltration into Assam and West Bengal.

“The narrative had been used to divide voters ahead of state elections in both states and to build support for the BJP,” he added.

For Gudavarthy, the issue points to a larger question about the strength of India’s democratic institutions.

“The system needs to be made accountable only through mass protests and institutional decentralisation,” he said. “It is a lesson for Indian democracy that institutions can be so easily subverted when there is executive overreach,” he added.
