item.title: Behind the white coats. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Medical college is where future doctors spend years mastering the art of saving lives. However, behind the intense study schedules and white coats lies a quiet mental health and behavioral crisis.
A nationwide study published in BMC Public Health reveals that nearly one in seven medical students in Bangladesh uses tobacco or other substances.
To understand the scope of this issue, our research team surveyed 1,129 medical students across 16 medical colleges in all eight divisions of Bangladesh. The findings provide important insights into the lives of our future healthcare professionals.
Overall, 13.64% of medical students reported using tobacco or other substances. Tobacco was the most commonly used product, accounting for 54.5%.
However, the study also found notable use of non-prescription & non-pharmacological use of sedatives (26%) and cough syrups containing codeine or dextromethorphan (18.8%).
Since these medications are sold over the counter, students can easily get them when they are stressed or can't sleep.
The data shows a clear upward trend throughout medical training. While only 4.9% of first-year students reported substance use, the figure climbs to 21.8% among final-year students and reaches 26% among intern doctors.
The relentless academic workload, long clinical rotations, and chronic exhaustion may become increasingly challenging as students progress through their medical training.
Key insights emerged regarding the psychosocial triggers behind substance use:
Perhaps the most alarming finding is the severe lack of institutional support. Over 35% of student users reported that no one had ever approached them to offer help with stopping.
Institutional interventions such as campus counseling or official support programs accounted for less than 0.6% of cessation efforts.
When asked why non-users refrained from substances, students cited religious values (68.3%), moral ethics (63.8%), and family reasons (39.8%) as their primary shields.
These protective factors offer valuable direction for designing prevention strategies.
Addressing this concern requires immediate, multi-tiered action:
Doctors are the backbone of our health system. Protecting their well-being during their formative training years is essential not only for their own lives, but for the quality of care they will provide to the nation.
Dr Shouvik Roy Subha is a medical doctor, public health researcher, and epidemiologist.

item.title: Why do foreign governments and lenders still want to invest in Bangladesh?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The IMF's October World Economic Outlook forecasts 3.2% growth for Bangladesh in FY27, down from 4.3% in April, with average inflation rising to 10.9%.
A week earlier, the World Bank cut its own forecast to 3.4% and said the weakness would persist through FY28, while it expects South Asia to grow at 6.9%.
If the IMF is right, this will be the slowest growth since FY1988-89, and place Bangladesh last among the seven South Asian economies in its table.
India is projected to grow at more than twice Bangladesh's rate. Sri Lanka, which defaulted on its external debt in 2022, is projected to grow faster than Bangladesh this year, as are Pakistan and Nepal. The medium-term outlook is weaker still, as the IMF projects Bangladesh's growth to fall to 2.2% in FY28 (Figure 1).
Yet over the same months, despite the grim forecasts for growth, the news from Dhaka has been of foreign governments and multilateral lenders showing strong interest in deepening their investments in Bangladesh.
The joint declaration of Bangladesh and China in June committed the two governments to modernize Mongla Port, develop a Chinese economic and industrial zone in Chittagong, and speed up the feasibility study for the Teesta project. In August, the Chinese ambassador said these projects could attract around 30 Chinese companies investing about $500 million.
Japan signed an Economic Partnership Agreement with Bangladesh in February and an emergency support loan for economic resilience and energy supply in June. Its plans now go further, as senior Japanese diplomats told The Hindu last week that Tokyo wants to build an industrial value chain around the JICA-financed deep-sea port at Matarbari, linking India's seven northeastern states, Nepal, Bhutan, and Myanmar to the Bay of Bengal. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is expected in Tokyo at the end of October to seek Japanese financing for a Matarbari industrial, port, and commercial hub for 2026-2031.
On October 13, the Dutch minister for foreign trade and development cooperation met the PM, who welcomed Dutch interest in the Teesta feasibility study. A senior US State Department adviser has said Bangladesh could soon become eligible for financing from the US international development finance corporation. South Korea expects its trade agreement with Bangladesh, still awaiting signature, to raise Korean investment.
The multilateral lenders show the same interest. Bangladesh is the largest borrower from the World Bank's International Development Association, with an exposure of $22.7bn as of March 2026. The ADB committed$2.685bn to Bangladesh in FY26. The relationship with the IMF is also intact.
The finance minister's statement on October 4 that he had cancelled the IMF program was read as an exit. In fact, the IMF confirmed in June that Bangladesh had applied for a new program, and in July, the finance minister said the two sides had agreed on its broad framework.
Little more than a week after his statement, the minister sought the support of the IMF and the World Bank in Bangkok. The government is leaving the program it inherited to negotiate new conditions. It is not leaving the fund.
Why would these governments and lenders want to invest in an economy that is not poised to perform?
My answer is that a market of more than 170 million people does not shrink when its growth rate does. That gives Bangladesh a bargaining position few countries with such a forecast have. The evidence from other countries supports four reasons.
Firstly , investors follow the size of a market more than its growth rate. In 2016, in the middle of a deep recession, Brazil still received about $78.9bn of foreign direct investment, nearly half of the inflows to Latin America.
The proposals for Bangladesh follow the same logic. The Invest Bangladesh pipeline is led by renewable energy and information technology, and the Chinese proposals include the Dhaka-Chittagong highway and waste-to-energy plants. These serve the domestic market.
By my own arithmetic, even 3.2% growth on an economy of about $470bn adds around $15bn of output in a year.
Secondly , governments compete for influence in large and well-placed countries. In 2015, Indonesia awarded the Jakarta-Bandung high-speed rail to China over Japan after China agreed to build it without an Indonesian government guarantee, while Japan had offered a loan at 0.1% interest.
Bangladesh sits in the same contest, as China, Japan, the Netherlands, and the United States all seek a role in its ports, rivers, and energy.
China and the Netherlands have both offered support on the Teesta feasibility study. Japan's answer is Matarbari, and its diplomats cite the Southern Economic Corridor linking Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam as the model.
Thirdly , supply chains are moving out of China. Vietnam drew a record $25.35bn in foreign direct investment in 2024 as manufacturers diversified, helped by its trade agreements and lower labour costs.
The agreement with Japan, China's zero-tariff treatment of Bangladeshi goods, and the planned agreement with South Korea give Bangladesh a similar platform.
Fourthly , multilateral lenders do not walk away from large borrowers. In 2024, Egypt secured an IMF program of $8 billion, a World Bank package of $6 billion and EU support of €7.4bn. In Nigeria, where I also work, the World Bank approved about $9.35bn between June 2023 and May 2026, after the government removed the petrol subsidy and unified the exchange rate. In my reading, the financing in both countries was tied to reform.
However, most of this interest is still a promise, not an investment.
Ashik Chowdhury, who now chairs Invest Bangladesh, said in June that the Chinese company’s proposals had not been verified. Of the $1.3bn pipeline his agency reported in September, only a little over $400m had reached the decision or implementation stage.
UNCTAD puts total foreign direct investment into Bangladesh in 2025 at $1.8bn, and the World Bank's own commitment fell to $820m in FY26, its lowest. Interest lapses if the government does not convert it.
To secure these investments, the Ministry of Finance should conclude the new IMF program quickly, as finance ministry officials themselves describe an active program as a seal of approval that unlocks other financing.
In return, the government should accept the IMF’s conditions on raising tax revenue. Bangladesh collects only 8.3% of GDP in tax, among the lowest ratios in the world. The IMF mission discussed measures to raise that ratio as early as July, and no lender will drop the condition.
Each G2G partnership also needs a single owner in government and a published timetable, as the published accounts of the declaration with China give no cost or date for Mongla, Chittagong, or Teesta.
Invest Bangladesh should publish a quarterly tracker of every proposal and its stage. The government should also hold to the five-year tax outlook it presented to Chinese investors.
Size is the reason an economy like Bangladesh always has room to turn around. The governments and lenders now showing interest are betting on the market, not on this year's growth rate.
However, the turnaround will not happen unless the government removes the constraints the World Bank has named: Gas and electricity shortages that disrupt industry, non-performing loans that reached 33.2% in June, and weak revenue collection.
The Matarbari plan also depends on relations with India, as the Maitri Bridge over the Feni river, the link to Tripura, is not operating.
The government will keep its bargaining position only if it turns this interest into signed investment before the investors look elsewhere.
Md Rubaiyath Sarwar is Managing Director of Innovision Consulting and Trustee at Panam Institute, an Economic Think-Tank .

item.title: Saudi Arabia executes man over crimes allegedly committed as a child. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Saudi Arabia executes man over crimes allegedly committed as a child

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 10/20/2026 - 10:13
Human Rights Watch says Hassan al-Faraj was convicted over offences allegedly committed at 14, while Yousef al-Manasif faces execution after a Supreme Court ruling
Saudi Shia women during a protest against the execution of cleric Nimr al-Nimr in Qatif, Saudi Arabia, 8 January 2016 (STR/AFP)
Off

Saudi Arabia has executed a man convicted of offences allegedly committed when he was a child, according to Human Rights Watch (HRW).

Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, who was executed on Saturday, was convicted of offences allegedly committed when he was 14 years old, including "meeting and developing friendships with other detained and wanted individuals". 

“The execution of Hassan al-Faraj is unconscionable compounded by alleged torture-tainted evidence and a well-documented record of unfair trials,” said Joey Shea, HRW’s senior Saudi Arabia researcher.

“With the Supreme Court’s recent decision, Yousef al-Manasif is also at serious risk of execution,” she added.

Faraj was arrested in 2017 and sentenced to death by Saudi Arabia’s Specialised Criminal Court in 2022, according to HRW. 

His lawyers have said that he had been tortured and forced to sign a confession used in the case. HRW also reported that he was held in solitary confinement. 

Yousef al-Manasif, who was convicted over alleged offences committed when he was 15 and 16, is also at risk of execution after the Supreme Court reportedly upheld his sentence, according to the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights (ESOHR). 

Manasif was arrested in April 2017. He was accused of participating in protests against the Saudi authorities’ treatment of the country’s Shia minority and attending funeral processions in 2011 and 2012, when he was 15 and 16.

Bangladesh seeks answers after Saudi Arabia executes two of its citizens without notice
Read More »

A 2024 opinion adopted by the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found that the detention of Faraj, Manasif and three other men -  Jawad Qureiris, Abdullah al-Derazi and Jalal al-Labbad - was arbitrary and that their proceedings involved serious fair-trial violations.

It said their detention violated several provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and called for their immediate release and compensation. 

Saudi Arabia’s government disputed the allegations, saying the claims were unfounded and that the country’s laws and procedures complied with international human rights standards.

The UN working group’s report said Manasif alleged that he had been physically and psychologically tortured in detention and coerced into signing confessions later used against him. 

Another defendant, Ali al-Mabyook, was sentenced to death over alleged offences that included attending funeral processions before he turned 18, according to HRW and court documents. 

Coerced confessions

His case has also drawn concern from rights groups over the use of counterterrorism legislation and allegations of coerced confessions. 

Qureiris was sentenced to death in 2022 over alleged offences that included acts committed as a minor, according to the UN working group.

The group’s opinion said he had alleged that he was tortured and held in solitary confinement for 270 days to force a confession.

Saudi authorities executed Ali al-Subaiti on 9 April 2026, according to the Saudi Press Agency.

HRW said he had been sentenced to death over alleged offences that included participating in a demonstration when he was 12. 

Saudi Arabia’s 2018 Juvenile Law and a 2020 executive order introduced protections against imposing the death penalty for certain offences committed by people under 18. 

HRW has argued that the protections do not adequately cover defendants prosecuted under the kingdom’s counterterrorism legislation, leaving some people convicted over alleged childhood offences at risk of execution. 

“Saudi Arabia’s execution spree, particularly for offences by children, shows no signs of slowing down in 2026,” Shea said.

“This underscores the urgent need for the international community to press the Saudi government to immediately halt executions and abolish the death penalty once and for all.”

“We are struggling.” “I can’t feed my family.” “ It’s getting really tough to get by.”
At first glance, these testimonies might seem to reflect quotes of an economy in depression or communities enduring the upheaval of war. However, they are the mundane realities of working-class households in Bangladesh - - a country neither at war nor in severe distress. Yet, the world seems to be maliciously devised in ways that consistently leave them at the short end of the stick.
The economic realities of Bangladesh - - institutional shortcomings coupled with rising inflation - - have left nearly 28% of people in poverty, according to a 2025 PPRC survey. For the sake of simplicity, poverty is often reduced to the notion of having limited financial means. But what if poverty is not just about having less money? What if, in the very act of struggling to make ends meet, the poor are made to pay relatively more for the same necessities that the wealthy can afford for less?
Oscar Lewis’s culture of poverty theorizes that poverty is a self-perpetuating cycle through attitudes, behaviour and values that emerge under conditions of persistent deprivation. However, the cycle of entrapment occurs in more insidious ways, specifically through concepts like poverty premium. Consider a kilogram of sugar - in retail, it costs around ৳ 110/kg; but in bulk, it is only ৳ 90/kg -- a 19% decrease.
Sugar is hardly an isolated case. We have found larger disparities across several essential goods. Masoor dal , for instance, showed a price difference of 45% between retail and bulk purchasing, while onion showed a gap of 44%. Rice, perhaps the most important staple product in our households, was around 36% cheaper when purchased in bulk. Atta and m aid a have shown similar differences, at roughly 37% and 34% respectively. Each of these comparisons is like for like: T he same product, of the same quality, priced on the same day. The only thing that changed was how much was bought.
a typical 4.26-person household, rice alone accounts for 42 kilograms of consumption monthly. Because of this sheer volume, even a modest price difference across several retail purchases can aggregate to a substantial monthly expense. In our household basket calculation, rice itself accounted for roughly Tk 1,303 of the Tk 1,815 in potential monthly savings, approximately 72% of the total.
Across the basket, the difference between retail and bulk purchasing amounted to Tk 1,815 per month for a household eating at national average levels, or Tk 21,780 per year. Among Bangladesh’s poorest households, whose monthly expenditure exceeds income by roughly Tk 3,817, the potential savings would represent nearly half of that deficit. While the numbers are staggering, they barely capture the harshness of reality : I f the poorest households live on about Tk 283 a day, how can they afford any bulk products? If they can’t do so individually, could they access them collectively?
This is the idea behind Shomobay . Within neighbourhoods , families pre-register their weekly requirements. Afterwards, their demands are aggregated. We buy in bulk from the nearest wholesaler and hand everything over the same day at a collection point, at close to the bulk price -- curbing any storage constraints. The family does not have to become a bulk buyer. Instead, Shomobay becomes the intermediary between all the customers of bulk products in the neighbourhood , establishing a collective initiative.
The aim is not to reinvent how groceries are bought, but to recalibrate the purchasing position of the household; and that is what Shomobay achieved in the first pilot.
Anwar, one of the participants in the pilot, stated, “If I could buy through Shomobay every week, my monthly savings would increase significantly.” Fatema, a mother of three, echoed the same sense of optimism, “Because of this initiative, after buying the household groceries, I still have enough money left to buy other things.” If each of the 15 pilot families bought the full basket this way every month, they would collectively save about ৳ 27,225 a month. Across 1,000 families, that becomes about ৳ 18 lakh a month, or more than ৳ 2 crore a year. For a single family, the saving is about twice what a year of food inflation adds to a family’s grocery bill. Over a year, it adds up to roughly 45 days of wages for a garment worker on minimum wage. Broken down to a single day, the saving comes to about ৳ 60. In the poorest tenth of households, that is close to what one person lives on in a day.
Bangladesh is not short of attempts to make groceries cheaper. While TCB provides subsidized lentils, oils and sugar, coverage has shrunk from 1 crore families to roughly 70 lakh after mass cancellations. Truck sales arrive irregularly, often with long queues. Buyers we spoke to also raised concerns of corruption, syndicates and poor quality. Additionally, newer state initiatives like the Family Card are barely accessible to the people who need it most.
Abroad, the idea of pooling demand has been tried at scale. India’s DealShare was once valued at $1.7 billion; by 2026, it was in sale talks worth around $90 million. Kenya’s Twiga Foods, which raised over $150 million, entered administration in August 2026. China’s community group buying startups ended in a price war. Each time, the model has broken down the same way: prices subsidized with investor money, expensive warehouses and delivery fleets, or credit that customers could not repay.
Shomobay is built to avoid all three. There is no subsidy, families pay the real bulk price. No warehouse, goods are bought and sold upfront. No credit, families pay upfront. Shomobay does not aim to replace TCB but rather to mitigate the shortcomings that it has been plagued with for years.
As we continue refining the model, Shomobay is building a wider presence beyond the neighbourhoods in which it operates. We envision Shomobay growing from neighbourhoods to cities, from cities to communities across Bangladesh, and eventually beyond Bangladesh, wherever households face the same fundamental disadvantage of paying more simply because they can afford to buy less.
Jaif Bin Morshed is a r esearch i ntern, PRI (Policy Research Institute) .

item.title: Freedom of expression is not a privilege granted by those in power. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The concerns raised by rights organizations and media advocates over the proposed changes to the Cyber Protection Act, 2026, deserve serious consideration. We agree that the government must recognize that any legislation intended to protect cyberspace must not become a tool for silencing dissent.
The proposed provisions concerning defamation, maligning, rumours, and misinformation are particularly worrying because vague definitions can easily be misused. When the law leaves too much room for interpretation, legitimate criticism, investigative journalism, and public-interest reporting may become grounds for legal harassment.
The possibility of arbitrary content restrictions and punitive action against media outlets makes these concerns even more pressing.
Bangladesh has already witnessed how cyber laws can be weaponized against journalists, critics, and ordinary citizens. We cannot allow a new legal framework to reproduce the same failures under a different name.
Changing governments must also mean changing the practices that undermine democratic rights. Otherwise, promises of reform amount to little more than rhetoric.
There is, of course, a need to address genuine cybercrime, online harassment, and other harmful activities, but these objectives must be pursued through clearly defined offences, due process, independent oversight, and meaningful safeguards for freedom of expression.
The government must consult journalists, legal experts, civil society organizations, and digital rights advocates before advancing legislation that affects the fundamental rights of millions.
More importantly, any and all further attempts to stifle our freedom of speech must be dealt with promptly and decisively. This requires more than assurances that a law will not be misused -- it requires enforceable protections, transparent procedures, and accountability whenever authorities overstep their powers.
Freedom of expression is not a privilege granted by those in power. It is a fundamental right that allows citizens to question authority and hold institutions accountable.
It's time the government shows us that it understands this distinction. We cannot keep repeating the same mistakes at the cost of our freedom of speech.

item.title: The rule of law cannot depend on who holds a weapon. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
State Minister Ishraque Hossain’s decision to resign -- following public outrage over footage of him brandishing a firearm during an anti-drug operation -- is an important development. However, his resignation must not be allowed to end the dialogue about his conduct or the responsibilities of elected representatives.
Let us be clear: Ishraque's actions were not part of a minister’s role, and under no circumstances can they be misconstrued as valid or acceptable.
Ministers are entrusted with political leadership and the responsibility of ensuring that state institutions function effectively. An elected government must strengthen relevant agencies, provide them with adequate resources, ensure that they can perform their duties without political interference, as well as hold them accountable if they fail to do so.
It must be understood: We have not elected MPs to take the law into their own hands, nor should the public be encouraged to view such conduct as a heroic demonstration of strength.
Allowing elected officials to assume law enforcement roles risks undermining established procedures, weakening institutional authority, and setting a dangerous precedent. The rule of law cannot depend on who holds a weapon or occupies a position of power.
Drug trafficking is most certainly a serious problem that demands sustained action. However, an effective anti-drug campaign must be conducted through lawful procedures, professional investigations, and accountable enforcement.
No individual, regardless of political position or stated intentions, should be exempt from these standards.
Ishraque’s resignation must also not be taken as a substitute for accountability. The circumstances surrounding the incident must be examined, and any violation must be addressed through due process.
Such conduct cannot be praised as decisive leadership or ignored because its stated objective is an important one.
Strong institutions, not individual displays of power, are what protect the public and build trust in the state. The government must demonstrate that elected representatives are expected to uphold the law, not bypass it.

item.title: In art, a wall of heritage and an artificial message of division. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Even before Bangladesh was born as an independent state, the country’s cultural arena has been a battleground. This fight is not waged with shields and swords. It has mainly been carried on through the narrative of “religion versus culture.” Should the ancient culture of the Bengali people, which bears the strong influence of Sanatani (Hindu), Buddhist and Islamic faiths, be the foundation of national and state identity in this land? Or should the character of this state rest only on the religious identity of its Muslim-majority citizens, where language and culture from the Arab-Persian region count for more than Bengal’s own culture?
There is no reason to doubt the narrow communal mindset hidden inside this debate and this division, and these days it is hardly hidden at all. It is also undeniable that this debate plays an important role in Bangladesh’s political divisions. Above all, it was through this very division that attempts were made in 1970 and 1971 to block the emergence of Bangladesh as an independent country. But the 1970 election and the Liberation War of 1971 defeated that effort, and Bangladesh was born on the basis of Bengali cultural identity.
Recent events show that the stirring-up of the country’s origin, identity and basis of existence through that narrow debate, which began after the 2024 change of power, has not yet died down. The anti-Liberation War mindset that raised its head under the interim Yunus government is now being revived. Those who destroyed the Sheikh Mujib Memorial Museum at Road 32 in Dhanmondi to erase the history of the Liberation War, and who vandalized sculptures related to Bangabandhu and the Liberation War across the country, are now trying to strike at the very foundation of independence by a new route.
Distortion of history
Recently, the walls along a road in Dhaka were decorated with portraits of some leading figures of Bengali culture. Many welcomed this initiative by the city authorities on the wall beside the Shilpakala Academy. But then a campaign began on social media whose language, underlying message and purpose have become very familiar since the 2024 uprising. However crude the campaign’s methods, its aim is clear: T o crack the country’s cultural identity, to create division on the basis of religion, and to move the country’s birth from 1971 back to 1947, presenting Bangladesh as a product of the “two-nation theory.”
Freedom of dissent is important in every democratic society, even when that dissent amounts to distorting history. But it would be wrong to call what has been going on in Bangladesh for the past two years merely free expression. Alongside the rewriting of the nation’s history, there has been destructive activity, extreme intolerance of and threats against the pro-Liberation War narrative, and even communally provocative statements.
Some people on social media have asked why portraits of Satyajit Ray or Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar were placed beside those of Bangladesh’s eminent artist Zainul Abedin, the actor Humayun Faridi or the national poet Kazi Nazrul Islam. Their argument is that Ray and Vidyasagar are not “Bangladeshi.” Those who say this surely understand very well that “Bangladeshi” identity is not the point here. These figures were chosen for their mountainous contributions to Bengali culture. That is exactly their problem. But there, communalism is visibly playing a big part.
Nazrul and the nation
For example, there is no fuss about the portrait of Kazi Nazrul Islam, Bangladesh’s national poet. There is no reason for any. Just as there should be no controversy over Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, there should be no objection to Nazrul either, because both are Bengali and both made extraordinary contributions to Bengali literature and culture. Like Vidyasagar, Kazi Nazrul Islam was also an Indian. So why object to one of them? Because he is Hindu?
Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman brought Nazrul to Bangladesh in 1972 and allotted a house in Dhanmondi for his whole family. Nazrul was not only a leading figure in Bengali-language literature; in the backdrop of the Liberation War, he was a source of inspiration for the people. Nazrul’s poems and songs gave the people courage and inspiration in 1971. After independence, the government of independent Bangladesh felt fulfilled at being able to bring him close, and the people were happy and proud to see him with their own eyes.
The tragedy was that Nazrul had lost his understanding and his speech many years before coming to Dhaka. How much he understood that he had come to Dhaka as a guest of a newly independent state is open to question. But it was probably because of the state honour he received in Dhaka that Nazrul’s family stayed on in Bangladesh.
Nazrul was born in India, spent his whole life in India, and was an Indian. He did not become a Bangladeshi overnight by spending the last four years of his life in Dhaka. Yet there is no controversy or question anywhere about declaring Nazrul the national poet of Bangladesh. There should not be. Likewise, there should be no question or controversy about adopting a song written by Rabindranath Tagore as the national anthem. But here too, out of exactly the same communal mindset, controversy has been created over Rabindranath, a follower of the Brahmo Samaj, and over his song “Amar Shonar Bangla.”
The drama and the police response
A drama of erasing Rabindranath’s portrait from the wall of the Shilpakala Academy was also staged recently. It has to be called a drama because, while a woman was about to deface Rabindranath’s portrait with ink, countless people were seen around her filming on their phones, and perhaps one or two were even live-streaming. At that very moment, a policeman ran up and stopped her!
The whole incident looked like a publicity stunt. But afterwards the police filed a “sedition” case against the woman and four people from her organization , arranging even more publicity for them. The communal mindset of an organization that exists in name only, expressed through vandalism, may be seen as a nuisance. But whether it is reasonable to treat it as outright “sedition” is a question that can certainly be asked.
Yet there is also a silver lining behind the dark cloud. On one hand, the police reaction seems excessive, especially when the alleged “crime” is essentially confined to a political statement. On the other hand, the authorities’ firmness deserves praise. Had the same incident happened under the Yunus government, the portraits of Satyajit Ray and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar might have been wiped off the Shilpakala Academy wall overnight. Perhaps the officials in charge at the city authority would have had to answer for it, and perhaps a job or two would have been at stake.
It goes without saying that the course of events will not stop here. The process of cutting the people of Bangladesh off from their cultural history and heritage, which began two years ago, will undoubtedly continue. Whether the government will confront this tendency, or stay indifferent like the Yunus government and in effect keep encouraging it, is a decision the BNP must make.
Instead of isolated reactions to isolated incidents and overreactions like the “sedition” case, it is time for the government to send a clear message. The foundation of Bangladesh’s birth is the language and culture of Bengalis irrespective of religion or caste. In the Bengali language, literature and the whole cultural arena, no division on the basis of religion, or of which side of the border someone was born on, is acceptable. The government must give this message clearly. Otherwise the possibility will remain that this artificial division turns into political, social and communal conflict.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Bangladesh seeks answers after Saudi Arabia executes two of its citizens without notice. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Bangladesh seeks answers after Saudi Arabia executes two of its citizens without notice

Submitted by Areeb Ullah on Mon, 10/19/2026 - 12:59
Dhaka said it was not informed by Saudi Arabia that it had executed the pair arrested in Mecca for 'indecent acts'
Bangladeshi workers sitting outside an airport after flights to Saudi Arabia were cancelled following a series of Houthi attacks in October (AFP/Piyas Biswas)
Off

Bangladesh is seeking answers on why Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca without telling Dhaka.

Last week, Saudi Arabia executed a male and a female Bangladeshi national after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” inside a mosque.

Riyadh did not provide further details on the acts the two Bangladeshi nationals allegedly committed or whether they had legal representation in the Gulf kingdom, according to local media reports.

Reacting to the incident, Bangladesh’s minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told reporters that he was “very disappointed” by the lack of communication and that Dhaka was seeking an explanation on why they were executed and not informed beforehand about the execution.

“We have sought an explanation from our friendly bilateral partner to look into the matter and know why the gap in information sharing and exchanges happened here. We are in discussions," he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday.

Earlier, the Bangladeshi foreign ministry said that it was waiting for a copy of the full verdict and the circumstances that led to the execution.

The official added that the two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh but did not indicate that they had planned to execute them.

Last week, Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court overturned the death sentence of a Sri Lankan national after he allegedly insulted Islam and the Prophet Muhammad.

Sri Lanka’s Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra confirmed that Riyadh had overturned the death sentence of Anojan Sivarasa.

The 27-year-old remains imprisoned after he was sentenced to five years in prison and fined three million Saudi Riyals ($800,000).

The court handed down the sentence amid intense criticism of Riyadh's legal system.

Saudi Arabia relies on interpretations of Islamic law, alongside cybercrime and counterterror legislation, to target online expression under the guise of protecting "public morals".

This has resulted in a surge of decades-long prison terms for social media users and an increased use of capital punishment.

At least 175 people have been executed so far this year, the majority of whom are foreign nationals.
